items.title: The central dogma of molecular biology
items.explainer: Francis Crick coined the phrase 'central dogma' in 1958 to describe how genetic information flows in cells. Information stored in DNA is copied into messenger RNA in a process called transcription, and the RNA sequence is then read by ribosomes and translated into a chain of amino acids that folds into a protein. The genetic code that links them is read in three-letter words called codons; with four nucleotide letters there are 64 possible codons, which specify 20 standard amino acids plus stop signals, so most amino acids are encoded by more than one codon. Crick's key claim was narrower than it is often presented: once information has passed into protein, it cannot flow back out into nucleic acid. Information can, however, flow from RNA back to DNA. Retroviruses such as HIV use an enzyme called reverse transcriptase, discovered in 1970, to copy their RNA genomes into DNA that is inserted into the host's chromosomes. The picture has also grown richer in other ways. Many RNA molecules are never translated at all and instead regulate genes or form parts of cellular machinery, and the mRNA vaccines deployed against COVID-19 work by delivering instructions directly at the RNA stage of the flow.

source.title: Central dogma of molecular biology - Wikipedia

question.prompt: Which information transfer does the central dogma, as Crick stated it, say is impossible?

options.text: From protein back to DNA or RNA

question.explanation: Crick's claim was that sequence information cannot flow out of protein. RNA-to-DNA transfer does occur, through reverse transcriptase.

items.title: CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing
items.explainer: CRISPR began as a bacterial immune system. Bacteria store short snippets of DNA from viruses that have attacked them in a region of their genome called CRISPR, transcribe those snippets into guide RNAs, and use them to direct Cas proteins to cut matching viral DNA if the virus returns. In 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that the Cas9 protein could be programmed with a single engineered guide RNA to cut almost any chosen DNA sequence, work for which they shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The guide RNA, about 20 nucleotides long, pairs with the target sequence, which must sit next to a short motif the protein recognizes. Cas9 then makes a double-strand break. The cell's own repair systems take over: error-prone repair often disrupts the gene, which is useful for switching genes off, while repair from a supplied template can write in a precise change. Newer variants called base editors and prime editors change individual letters without a full double-strand break, reducing unwanted damage. In late 2023, regulators in the United Kingdom and the United States approved the first CRISPR-based therapy, for sickle cell disease. Off-target cuts at similar sequences remain a key safety concern.

question.prompt: What determines which DNA sequence the Cas9 protein cuts?

options.text: The shape of the Cas9 protein alone
A guide RNA that base-pairs with the target sequence
The temperature at which the edit is performed

question.explanation: Cas9 is directed by its guide RNA; changing the roughly 20-nucleotide guide sequence retargets the cut to a different site.

items.title: Natural selection and fitness
items.explainer: Natural selection, described by Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace in 1858, follows from three observations. Individuals in a population vary; some of that variation is inherited; and more offspring are produced than can survive and reproduce. Individuals whose inherited traits suit them better to their environment tend, on average, to leave more offspring, so those traits become more common over generations. In biology, 'fitness' has a specific meaning that differs from everyday usage: it is reproductive success, the relative number of offspring an individual contributes to the next generation, not strength or health as such. A strong animal that leaves no offspring has a fitness of zero. Selection acts only on variation that already exists; it does not create traits because they are needed. New variation arises from random mutation and from the reshuffling of genes during sexual reproduction. Selection is also not the only force that changes populations. Genetic drift, random change in gene frequencies, can dominate in small populations, and migration moves genes between populations. Selection can be observed directly today. Bacteria evolve antibiotic resistance within months, insects evolve resistance to pesticides, and the beaks of Darwin's finches in the Galapagos have measurably changed in size after droughts altered the available seeds.

question.prompt: In evolutionary biology, what does 'fitness' measure?

options.text: Relative reproductive success: the offspring contributed to the next generation

question.explanation: Fitness is about passing on genes. Traits like strength or longevity matter only insofar as they affect the number of surviving offspring.

items.title: Mitochondria and endosymbiosis
items.explainer: Mitochondria are the organelles that produce most of a cell's usable energy, generating ATP by oxidizing nutrients in a process that consumes oxygen. They also have a remarkable origin. According to endosymbiotic theory, championed by the biologist Lynn Margulis from 1967 onward, mitochondria descend from free-living bacteria that were engulfed by an ancestral host cell more than a billion years ago. Rather than being digested, the bacteria survived inside the host, and over time the two became completely dependent on each other. Several lines of evidence support the theory. Mitochondria have two membranes, consistent with a bacterium wrapped in a host membrane. They carry their own small, circular DNA genome, as bacteria do, and they divide by a fission-like process rather than being built from scratch. Their ribosomes resemble bacterial ribosomes more than the host's, and gene sequencing places them close to a particular group of bacteria. Chloroplasts in plants have a similar origin from photosynthetic cyanobacteria. In humans, mitochondrial DNA is inherited almost entirely from the mother, which makes it a powerful tool for tracing maternal ancestry. Mutations in mitochondrial DNA cause a range of inherited diseases that affect energy-hungry tissues such as muscle and the brain.

question.prompt: Which observation supports the theory that mitochondria descended from bacteria?

options.text: Mitochondria are found only in plant cells
Mitochondria are assembled from scratch by the nucleus
Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and bacteria-like ribosomes

question.explanation: Their own circular genome, bacterial-type ribosomes, double membrane and division by fission all point to a bacterial ancestor.

items.title: The action potential
items.explainer: Neurons communicate along their length using brief electrical pulses called action potentials. At rest, the inside of a neuron is about 70 millivolts negative relative to the outside, a voltage maintained by pumps that move sodium out of the cell and potassium in. When incoming signals push the membrane voltage above a threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open, sodium ions rush in, and the inside briefly becomes positive. Within about a millisecond the sodium channels inactivate and voltage-gated potassium channels open, letting potassium flow out and restoring the negative resting voltage. The pulse is all-or-none: a stimulus either triggers a full-size action potential or none at all, so neurons encode intensity through the frequency of firing rather than the size of individual spikes. Each spike triggers the next patch of membrane, so the signal travels along the axon without fading. Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley worked out this mechanism using the giant axon of the squid, work recognized with a Nobel Prize in 1963. Many axons are wrapped in insulating myelin, which forces the signal to jump between gaps, greatly increasing conduction speed. In multiple sclerosis, damage to myelin slows or blocks these signals, producing the disease's varied neurological symptoms.

question.prompt: What causes the rapid rising phase of a neuron's action potential?

options.text: Voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium ions flow into the cell
Potassium ions flow into the cell
The sodium-potassium pump suddenly reverses direction

question.explanation: Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels lets positive sodium ions rush in, driving the membrane potential from negative to positive.

items.title: Enzymes and Michaelis-Menten kinetics
items.explainer: Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly proteins, that speed up chemical reactions in cells by binding their reactants, called substrates, in an active site shaped to stabilize the reaction's transition state. In 1913 Leonor Michaelis and Maud Menten described how the rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction depends on substrate concentration. At low substrate concentrations the rate rises almost in proportion to the amount of substrate. At high concentrations the enzyme molecules are nearly all occupied, and the rate levels off at a maximum, Vmax, set by how many enzyme molecules are present and how fast each one works. The Michaelis constant, Km, is the substrate concentration at which the rate reaches half of Vmax. A low Km means the enzyme reaches half its maximal speed at a low substrate concentration, which often, though not always, reflects tight binding. These two parameters are central to pharmacology and drug discovery. A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and competes with the substrate, raising the apparent Km without changing Vmax, because enough substrate can still outcompete it. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and lowers Vmax. Many drugs, including statins that lower cholesterol, work as enzyme inhibitors.

question.prompt: How does a classic competitive inhibitor affect an enzyme's kinetic parameters?

options.text: It lowers Vmax but leaves Km unchanged
It raises the apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged
It lowers both Km and Vmax
It has no effect on either parameter

question.explanation: A competitive inhibitor competes for the active site; more substrate is needed to reach half-maximal rate, but at very high substrate the inhibitor is outcompeted, so Vmax is unchanged.

items.title: Gene regulation and the lac operon
items.explainer: Every cell in your body carries essentially the same DNA, yet a liver cell and a neuron behave completely differently, because cells control which genes are switched on. The first mechanism of gene regulation to be worked out was the lac operon of the bacterium E. coli, described by Francois Jacob and Jacques Monod in 1961, work honored with a Nobel Prize in 1965. The operon is a set of genes needed to use the sugar lactose. Using them costs energy, so the bacterium makes the enzymes only when they are useful. When lactose is absent, a repressor protein binds to a DNA region called the operator and blocks transcription. When lactose is present, a form of it binds the repressor, changing its shape so it releases the DNA, and the genes are transcribed. A second layer of control involves glucose, the bacterium's preferred fuel. When glucose is scarce, a signaling molecule called cyclic AMP accumulates and helps an activator protein boost transcription. The genes are therefore expressed strongly only when lactose is present and glucose is absent. This logic of repressors, activators and DNA switches turned out to be a general principle, and far more elaborate versions control development and cell identity in plants and animals.

question.prompt: Under which conditions are the lac operon genes expressed most strongly?
question.explanation: Lactose removes the repressor, and the absence of glucose allows cyclic AMP to activate transcription, so both conditions are needed for strong expression.

items.title: Meiosis and genetic variation
items.explainer: Meiosis is the specialized cell division that produces eggs and sperm. A human body cell carries 23 pairs of chromosomes, one set inherited from each parent. Meiosis halves that number, so each egg or sperm carries a single set of 23, and fertilization restores the full complement of 46. Beyond halving the chromosome number, meiosis is a powerful generator of genetic variation, through two mechanisms. The first is independent assortment. When the chromosome pairs separate, each pair splits independently of the others, so each gamete receives a random mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes. With 23 pairs, that alone allows 2 to the 23rd power, about 8.4 million, different combinations from each parent. The second mechanism is crossing over. Before they separate, the paired chromosomes exchange segments, creating new combinations of gene variants along each chromosome. Together with the random pairing of a particular egg and sperm, these processes make every child genetically unique, apart from identical twins. Errors in meiosis also matter medically. If a chromosome pair fails to separate properly, a gamete ends up with an extra or missing chromosome. Down syndrome most often results from such an error, which leaves an extra copy of chromosome 21.

question.prompt: How many chromosome combinations can independent assortment alone produce in a single human's gametes?
question.explanation: Each of the 23 chromosome pairs can send either member to a gamete independently, giving 2^23, about 8.4 million, combinations before crossing over adds more.

items.title: Horizontal gene transfer
items.explainer: Most organisms pass genes vertically, from parent to offspring. Bacteria can also exchange genes horizontally, between unrelated cells and even between different species, and this ability makes them extraordinarily adaptable. There are three main routes. In transformation, a bacterium takes up free DNA from its surroundings, often released by dead cells; Frederick Griffith's 1928 experiments with pneumonia bacteria first revealed this. In transduction, a virus that infects bacteria accidentally packages some host DNA and delivers it to the next cell it infects. In conjugation, one bacterium transfers DNA directly to another through a thin bridge, usually in the form of a plasmid, a small circle of DNA separate from the main chromosome. Horizontal gene transfer is the main reason antibiotic resistance spreads so quickly. A resistance gene that arises in one harmless species can be carried on a plasmid into a dangerous pathogen, and a single plasmid may carry resistance to several drugs at once. Hospitals, farms that use antibiotics heavily, and wastewater are hotspots for such exchange. Horizontal transfer is not limited to bacteria: part of the human genome derives from ancient viral infections, and some genes appear to have moved between distantly related plants and animals.

question.prompt: Which mechanism moves DNA directly from one bacterium to another through a physical connection, often carrying plasmids?
question.explanation: Conjugation uses direct cell-to-cell contact; transformation uses free DNA from the environment and transduction uses viruses as carriers.

items.title: Homeostasis and negative feedback
items.explainer: Homeostasis is the body's ability to keep internal conditions such as temperature, blood pH and blood glucose within narrow ranges despite a changing environment. Most homeostatic systems work by negative feedback: a sensor detects a deviation from a set point, and a response pushes the variable back toward it, much as a thermostat switches on the heating when a room cools. Blood glucose regulation is a clear example. After a meal, rising glucose prompts beta cells in the pancreas to release insulin, which signals muscle, fat and liver cells to take up glucose and store it, bringing levels back down. Between meals, falling glucose prompts alpha cells in the pancreas to release glucagon, which tells the liver to release stored glucose. In a healthy person, fasting blood glucose is usually kept at roughly 70 to 100 milligrams per deciliter. When feedback breaks down, disease follows. In type 1 diabetes the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells; in type 2 diabetes the body's cells respond poorly to insulin. Positive feedback, which amplifies a change instead of reversing it, is less common and usually drives a process to completion, as in blood clotting or the escalating contractions of childbirth.

question.prompt: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, which response brings blood glucose back down?

options.text: The pancreas releases glucagon, prompting the liver to release glucose
The pancreas releases insulin, prompting cells to take up glucose
Body temperature rises to burn the excess sugar

question.explanation: Rising glucose triggers insulin release from pancreatic beta cells; insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, a negative-feedback response.

items.title: Photosynthesis
items.explainer: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae and cyanobacteria capture the energy of sunlight and store it in sugar. Overall, six molecules of carbon dioxide and six of water become one molecule of glucose and six of oxygen, but the work happens in two linked stages inside chloroplasts. In the light-dependent reactions, which take place in the thylakoid membranes, the pigment chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light; green light is largely reflected, which is why leaves look green. The absorbed energy is used to split water molecules, releasing oxygen as a by-product, and to make two energy carriers, ATP and NADPH. In the second stage, the Calvin cycle, which runs in the fluid around the thylakoids, these carriers power the fixing of carbon dioxide from the air into sugars. The key enzyme, RuBisCO, is thought to be the most abundant protein on Earth. It is also slow and sometimes grabs oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, a wasteful reaction that some plants, such as maize and sugar cane, limit by concentrating carbon dioxide around it, a strategy known as C4 photosynthesis. Photosynthesis is the source of almost all the oxygen in the atmosphere and of the energy in nearly every food chain.

question.prompt: Where does the oxygen released by photosynthesis come from?
question.explanation: In the light-dependent reactions water is split to supply electrons, releasing its oxygen as a by-product.

items.title: Cellular respiration and ATP
items.explainer: Cells run on adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, a small molecule that acts as the energy currency of life. Breaking off its last phosphate group releases energy that powers muscle contraction, nerve signals and the building of new molecules. Cellular respiration is how cells recharge their ATP by breaking down food, mainly glucose, in three main stages. Glycolysis, in the cytoplasm, splits each glucose into two molecules of pyruvate and makes a small net gain of two ATP; it needs no oxygen. In the presence of oxygen, pyruvate enters the mitochondria and is broken down in the citric acid cycle, also called the Krebs cycle, which releases carbon dioxide and loads high-energy electrons onto carrier molecules. Finally, in oxidative phosphorylation, those electrons pass along a chain of proteins in the inner mitochondrial membrane, pumping protons across it. The protons flow back through the enzyme ATP synthase, a rotating molecular motor that makes most of the cell's ATP. Oxygen is the last stop for the electrons and combines with protons to form water. Altogether one glucose molecule yields roughly 30 to 32 ATP. Without oxygen, cells fall back on fermentation, producing lactate in human muscle or ethanol in yeast, for only the two ATP from glycolysis.

question.prompt: Which stage of cellular respiration produces most of the cell's ATP?

options.text: Oxidative phosphorylation, driven by ATP synthase

question.explanation: Glycolysis yields only two ATP; most of the roughly 30 ATP per glucose comes from the proton flow through ATP synthase.

items.title: DNA replication
items.explainer: Every time a cell divides, it must copy its entire genome, more than three billion base pairs in a human cell, accurately. James Watson and Francis Crick noted in 1953 that the double helix suggests how: the two strands are complementary, A pairing with T and G with C, so each strand can serve as a template for a new partner. Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl confirmed in 1958 that replication is semi-conservative, meaning each new double helix keeps one old strand and gains one new one. The enzyme helicase unwinds the helix, creating a replication fork. DNA polymerase then adds nucleotides matching the template, but it can only build in one direction and needs a short RNA primer to start. As a result, one strand, the leading strand, is made continuously, while the other, the lagging strand, is made in short pieces called Okazaki fragments, which DNA ligase later joins. DNA polymerase also proofreads its work, removing wrongly paired bases as it goes. Together with separate repair systems, this keeps the error rate to roughly one mistake per billion bases copied. Replication starts at many origins along each human chromosome at once, which is how the whole genome can be copied in a few hours.

question.prompt: What does it mean that DNA replication is semi-conservative?

options.text: Each new double helix contains one original strand and one newly made strand
Only half the genome is copied
Errors are kept in half of the copies
Replication stops halfway through the cell cycle

question.explanation: Meselson and Stahl showed each daughter molecule keeps one parental strand and gains one new strand.

items.title: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
items.explainer: The Hardy-Weinberg principle describes what happens to gene variants in a population when nothing is pushing them to change. Suppose a gene has two alleles, A and a, with frequencies p and q that add up to one. If mating is random, the population is large, and there is no selection, mutation or migration, then the genotype frequencies settle at p squared for AA, 2pq for Aa, and q squared for aa, and they stay there generation after generation. Godfrey Hardy and Wilhelm Weinberg worked this out independently in 1908. The principle matters because real populations rarely meet its assumptions, so departures from the expected frequencies are clues that evolution is happening, whether through natural selection, genetic drift in small populations, migration or non-random mating. It is also a practical tool. If a recessive genetic condition affects one in 2,500 newborns, then q squared is 1/2,500, so q is 1/50, and the share of healthy carriers, 2pq, is about one in 25. This kind of calculation is used in genetic counseling and in checking the quality of genetic data, where large deviations from Hardy-Weinberg proportions can reveal genotyping errors rather than biology.

question.prompt: A recessive condition affects 1 in 10,000 people in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Roughly what share are carriers?

items.title: Epigenetics
items.explainer: Every cell in your body carries essentially the same DNA, yet a liver cell and a neuron look and behave completely differently. Part of the explanation is epigenetics: chemical marks on DNA and its packaging that switch genes on or off without changing the DNA sequence itself. One major mark is DNA methylation, the addition of a methyl group to cytosine bases, usually where a cytosine is followed by a guanine. Heavy methylation near a gene's start tends to silence it. Another is the modification of histones, the proteins that DNA wraps around. Adding acetyl groups to histones loosens the packaging and makes genes easier to read; other marks pack DNA more tightly. These patterns are copied when cells divide, so a skin cell's descendants remain skin cells. Epigenetic marks can also respond to the environment. Studies of people conceived during the Dutch famine of 1944 to 1945 found differences in methylation of certain genes decades later. Epigenetic errors play a role in cancer, where tumor suppressor genes can be silenced by abnormal methylation, and some leukemia drugs work by removing those marks. How far epigenetic changes pass from parents to children in humans is still debated.

question.prompt: What is the defining feature of an epigenetic change?

options.text: It changes gene activity without changing the DNA sequence
It is always inherited by offspring

question.explanation: Epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation and histone modifications regulate gene activity while leaving the sequence intact.

items.title: Apoptosis
items.explainer: Apoptosis is programmed cell death, an orderly process by which cells kill themselves when they are no longer needed or have become dangerous. Unlike necrosis, the messy death of injured cells that burst and trigger inflammation, an apoptotic cell shrinks, condenses its DNA, chops itself into neat membrane-wrapped fragments and displays signals that invite immune cells to eat it. The work is done by caspases, enzymes that cut other proteins at specific sites. They can be activated by two main routes. In the intrinsic pathway, internal stress such as DNA damage causes mitochondria to release cytochrome c, which switches on the caspase cascade; proteins of the BCL-2 family decide whether this happens. In the extrinsic pathway, signal molecules from other cells bind death receptors on the cell surface. Apoptosis is essential for development: the webbing between human fingers disappears before birth because those cells die on schedule. It also removes immune cells that would attack the body. Too little apoptosis lets damaged cells survive and is a hallmark of cancer, and the drug venetoclax treats some leukemias by blocking BCL-2 so cancer cells can die again. Too much contributes to neurodegenerative diseases. Sydney Brenner, Robert Horvitz and John Sulston shared the 2002 Nobel Prize for work on its genetics.

question.prompt: How does apoptosis differ from necrosis?

options.text: Apoptosis causes the cell to burst and triggers inflammation
They are two names for the same process
Apoptosis is an orderly, regulated self-destruction that avoids inflammation

question.explanation: Apoptotic cells dismantle themselves into tidy fragments cleared by immune cells, whereas necrotic cells burst and inflame tissue.

items.title: Circadian rhythms
items.explainer: Most living things, from bacteria to people, have an internal clock that runs on a cycle of roughly 24 hours. These circadian rhythms govern when we feel sleepy, when body temperature peaks and when hormones such as cortisol and melatonin are released. The clock keeps running even without outside cues: people living in caves with no daylight still follow a cycle, although it drifts slightly from 24 hours. In mammals the master clock is the suprachiasmatic nucleus, a small cluster of neurons in the hypothalamus that receives light signals directly from the eyes and keeps clocks in other organs in step. Light, especially in the morning, is the strongest cue for resetting it each day. At the molecular level, the clock is a feedback loop. Clock genes are switched on and their proteins build up, then those proteins return to the nucleus and shut down their own genes, until they are broken down and the cycle starts again. Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael Young won the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for uncovering this loop in fruit flies. Jet lag and shift work disrupt the clock, and long-term disruption has been linked to poorer sleep, metabolism and health.

question.prompt: What is the strongest environmental cue for resetting the human circadian clock?

options.text: Light, acting through the eyes on the suprachiasmatic nucleus

question.explanation: Light signals from the retina reach the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the master clock, and reset it daily.

items.title: Telomeres and cellular aging
items.explainer: The ends of our chromosomes are capped by telomeres, long stretches of a short DNA sequence, TTAGGG in humans, repeated thousands of times and bound by protective proteins. They solve two problems. First, they stop the cell from mistaking a chromosome end for a broken piece of DNA that needs repair. Second, they act as a buffer for the end-replication problem: because DNA polymerase needs a primer to start, it cannot copy the very tip of a chromosome, so a little telomere is lost every time a cell divides. When telomeres become too short, the cell stops dividing and enters senescence, or dies. Leonard Hayflick observed in the 1960s that normal human cells in culture divide only about 40 to 60 times; shortening telomeres help explain this limit. Some cells, such as stem cells and those in the germline, use the enzyme telomerase to rebuild their telomeres. Elizabeth Blackburn, Carol Greider and Jack Szostak shared the 2009 Nobel Prize for discovering how telomeres and telomerase work. About 85 to 90 percent of cancers switch telomerase back on, which lets their cells divide indefinitely. Telomere length is linked with aging, but it is only one of many factors, and lengthening telomeres is not a proven way to slow aging.

question.prompt: Why do most cancers reactivate telomerase?

options.text: To repair mutations in their genes
To rebuild their telomeres so their cells can keep dividing indefinitely

question.explanation: Without telomerase, telomeres shorten with each division until the cell stops dividing; telomerase removes that limit.

items.title: Osmosis and membrane transport
items.explainer: Every cell is wrapped in a membrane made of a double layer of lipids, which lets some substances through and blocks others. Small, uncharged molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide slip across by simple diffusion, moving from where they are more concentrated to where they are less. Water crosses too, largely through channel proteins called aquaporins, and its movement across a membrane from a dilute solution towards a more concentrated one is called osmosis. If a red blood cell is placed in pure water, water rushes in and the cell swells and can burst; in very salty water, water leaves and the cell shrivels. This is why intravenous drips use saline with about the same salt concentration as blood. Charged ions and larger molecules such as glucose need help. In facilitated diffusion, carrier or channel proteins let them move down their concentration gradient without using energy. Active transport moves substances against their gradient and needs energy, usually from ATP. The most famous example is the sodium-potassium pump, which pushes three sodium ions out of the cell and two potassium ions in for each ATP it uses. It consumes a large share of the body's energy and sets up the gradients that nerves use to fire.

question.prompt: What happens to a red blood cell placed in pure water?

options.text: It swells and may burst as water enters by osmosis
It actively pumps the water out with no change

question.explanation: Pure water is more dilute than the cell's interior, so water moves in by osmosis until the cell swells or bursts.

items.title: Speciation
items.explainer: Speciation is the evolutionary process by which one species splits into two. Under the widely used biological species concept, species are groups that can interbreed with each other but not with other groups, so speciation is really about how barriers to interbreeding arise. The most common route is allopatric speciation, in which a population is divided by a geographic barrier, such as a mountain range, a river changing course or the colonization of an island. The separated populations then accumulate different mutations and face different selection pressures, and given enough time they become so different that they could no longer interbreed even if reunited. Darwin's finches on the Galápagos Islands, descended from a single ancestor that arrived from the mainland, are a classic example. Speciation can also happen without a physical barrier, called sympatric speciation, for example when insects shift to a new host plant and begin mating only on it, or when plants double their chromosome number, which can create a new species in a single generation. Reproductive barriers include mating at different times, incompatible courtship signals and hybrid offspring that are sterile; a mule, from a horse and a donkey, is usually sterile, so horses and donkeys remain separate species.

question.prompt: What is the key event in allopatric speciation?

options.text: A single mutation creates a new species overnight in animals
A population is split by a geographic barrier and the parts diverge

question.explanation: Geographic separation stops gene flow, letting each population diverge until they can no longer interbreed.
